After a rather chaotic start, double patrol to Strmica for the crater analysis after the false alarm at 0030 hours. Samuel, Alfons, Felix, and I were up in the middle of the night, despite the curfew to report on the shelling, but then only to HQ. On Sunday morning, we drove to Strmica for the crater analysis. We picked up the LO at the Northern Dalmatia Corps, but then there was artillery shelling from Strmica on the western side of the hill about one kilometre away." Now, yesterday, in your testimony at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, there is the page 3183. And if you want to pull up the words "provided support," I think could you find it, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just correct a portion of the reading, I believe the document actually says: "There is was shelling on the western hillside, about one kilometre away." I think Mr. Kehoe read it as "on the west side of the hill," which I think it is two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that, and I did not find it a reason to intervene, but you have drawn our attention to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony yesterday, you noted on line 22 -- actually in two locations. You noted on line 22 and 21: "And after the shelling, we did not investigate the areas that were to the west that provided support during the shelling." Now, in looking at your testimony yesterday, and then Mr. Marti's diary, was there outgoing shelling by the ARSK while you were up there on the 30th of July?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The RSK did not fire. There was no fire coming from their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, when you told us yesterday that the area to the west provided support during the shelling, is it your testimony this there was no firing from that area?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not utter anything of the sort yesterday. Perhaps, it was wrongly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have said anything yesterday about the response fire coming from the RSK because there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also noted that, previously, you hadn't picked up any other ARSK officer. Let's continue down on this. You said: "After waiting at the roadside, we continued at the edge of Strmica. We picked up Colonel Dokovic." Do you recall that now, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my statement. This is the statement of Peter Marti. My statement is that we picked up the liaison officer in Knin. Why there are discrepancies? Well, after the first shells, the -- or, rather, the liaison officer was with us with the car. After the first shells fell down, he jumped out of the car, went to the first shelter which was right next to the road, and hid over there. We started turning our vehicle around, and we drove away. After some time passed, one of our cars went back to pick up the colonel, the liaison officer. For the rest of the journey, he was with us. This is simply a nuance that Peter didn't explain sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you did, in fact, have a Colonel Dokovic with you as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what do you mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As well as the liaison officer that they picked up from the Northern Dalmatia Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, but that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the liaison officer that accompanied you, was that a Colonel Dokovic or that was any other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the last name, but his rank was that of a colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was one person with you, not two persons, the one who you picked up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with this. Now, there was -- Mr. Marti then says: "Then there was more artillery shelling that caused to us take shelter at the farmhouse along the road." So was there a second episode of shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I testified about that. As soon as we arrived to the northern positions of the Kenyan Battalion, the first shells landed, the first explosions took place. It was precisely then that the colonel jumped out of the car and hid. We started turning our cars and driving back, and then one of our cars went back to pick up the colonel. Then these shells started falling again, and we were forced to abandon our cars and to seek shelter in one of the neighbouring houses. It was a case where this shelling lasted for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, just on that point, and with Mr. Marti's comment on that and this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the sake much clarity, I will just give the statement of Mr. Marti of December 14th, 2007 at paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He notes: "I have recorded in my diary on 30 July ..." this is at paragraph 28, "... 30 July, that on the way to conduct a crater analysis in Strmica, we came under fire from five or six shells. The shells were coming from the east, from the direction of Grahovo. There was a Serbian check-point nearby, but I cannot say what the target was meant to be." Is it your testimony that it was more than five or six shells as was told by Mr. Marti to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're apparently quoting from a portion which is not available to us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can, I will bring up it just for demonstrative purposes, Judge. It is 1D23-0002, and that would be paragraph 28 of that document. It is one, two, three, four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not his diary but apparently a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A statement given to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 28. If we could just highlight paragraph 28. That 's what I read, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony, Mr. Tchernetsky, this was more than five or six shells?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first instance of shelling was precisely as you described. It is my understanding that Peter Marti described in this instance first salvo, and then the shelling continued for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to D163, quickly. Your Honour, I will tender the actual excerpt from the diary, which is 1D23-0021 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D224 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can now just bring D163, page 2, bottom paragraph: "D, Sector South."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes that: "The situation in the sector remains tense, especially in Sector East corner of the sector, where 115 artillery shells were fired or impacted: 30 HV, 88 RSK." Another sentence down: "The ARSK are reacting to the events in Bosansko Grahovo by deploying forces. However, the HV so far does not appear to close with or cross the border. The sector assessed the Croatian efforts. In the face of ARSK, opposition as unlikely in the Dinara. The situation at Strmica is being monitoring closely to foresee the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which might spill over into the sector and ensure the security of UN troops." As an UNMO --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll let the translation go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As an UNMO, Mr. Tchernetsky, did you learn the firing point of the RSK for those 88 rounds that they fired?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the next -- that next couple of lines down. Did you learn during the course of your time that, in late July, the RSK was reacting to owe vents in Bosansko Grahovo by redeploying forces. Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment here, Judge. Sorry to people in the interpretation booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me change the subject matter here, given that I don't have much time, sir. Now, you noted, during the course of your witness statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just for your information, you have got until 12.55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I thought it was Christmas, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying on this particular topic, moving to the topic of information, you noted that you were in the area of Bosansko Grahovo where you maintain that you found some documentation concerning the shelling by the HV. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was much later, after Operation Storm. In joint patrolling together with the representative of the sector staff, as far as I remember, Danish Captain Thomas, we got assignments from the senior UNMO to try to penetrate Grahovo from the side of Strmica. However, at the entrance to Grahovo we were stopped, then we attempted to drive through mountain paths, mountain tracks. And not far away from one of the roads in the woods, we found an abandoned headquarters of what we presumed was an artillery unit, where we found documents and a number of other items, including supplies, abandoned sights, aiming devices, et cetera. It was before the border. We did not cross the border with Bosnia, and we were not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, when was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what was your job up there, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our assignment that we were given was to assess the consequences of the operation and the level of damage to the town of Bosansko Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you were not in Bosnia -- let me back that up. You say -- you told the Office of the Prosecutor that your Senior Military Observer did not want to include the information that you had in a sitrep because he thought that you would -- or they would be accused of spying, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. Because those were Croatian documents, they were marked secret, and that's why he refused to include them in the daily report. Instead, he suggested to me that I drive them to the headquarters of our mission in Zagreb, which I did the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you maintain that you were not in Bosnia when you did this. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, no. It was before the border with Bosnia. We didn't cross the border. The border goes along the mountain range, and we were this side of the mountain range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony now, sir, that you were not in Bosnia at the time, but Steinar Hjertnes didn't want that stuff -- those items published anyway? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot now be precise about the location where the Danish captain and I found this abandoned headquarters. But, Steinar, yes, the documents were Croatian, they were marked "secret," and that is why Steinar didn't want to take the responsibility of including them in his report. Instead, he instructed me to turn them over personally, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you don't have them now, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I turned them over to the headquarters of our mission. I reported to the deputy of the chief military observer, an English Colonel. I cannot remember his name now, and he turned it over to the information department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can have the map that Mr. Russo turned over, about the area where Mr. Tchernetsky found these items.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I can assist. I actually have a portion of this that I had intended to go into, so I did another one of those blow-ups for this. It is 65 ter 4940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at it and then, Mr. Kehoe, tell us whether it's a useful excerpt from this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I will tender to the Court, during the proofing session, we received a document that was marked by the witness that clearly showed that it was in Bosnia, and I will tender that back to the Trial Chamber. But this is not the document that was tendered to us by the Office of the Prosecutor from the proofing session. But we will offer that across the bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not load that map into e-court. I was going to have him actually mark it here in court on this particular exhibit, in order to save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's been, Mr. Tchernetsky, quite a lot of discussion on whether you found the items in Bosnia and Herzegovina or not. Did I understand your testimony well when you said -- when I heard you saying that you thought you would still be in Croatia or at least in the -- but that you're not certain about that. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I do, in fact, have a copy of what the -- was tendered to us in the supplemental information sheet of 18 May 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way or is there any dispute about whether it was on the Croatian side of the border or on the Bosnian side of the border, and how vital is the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I, quite frankly, don't know what the confrontation line was on that particular day was, but I certainly disagree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we're talking about state borders, rather than about confrontation lines, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no idea. I have no dispute about whether or not it was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, if the Defence takes the position that it would have been in Bosnia, you would not challenge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll move on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tchernetsky, with this document, you didn't keep a copy, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't make copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you have not been shown any copies of that during the course of your meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor, have you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copies of those documents that I found, or, rather, we found, were turned over to the headquarters, and I never saw them again. In the course of proofing, I was not shown copies of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you say that "we" turned them over to the headquarters, who is the "we" -- excuse me. That "we" found and turned over, who is the "we"?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, again, that I was accompanied by a representative of the Sector South headquarters, Captain Thomas from Denmark, to the best of my recollection. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in P205, your supplemental statement of 6 December 2007, you note in paragraph 8: "The Croatian maps and artillery plans showed enemy positions that did not, in fact, exist. Specifically, they showed enemy positions in areas which I knew personally -- excuse me, I personally knew to be entirely civilian without any military targets. "Although I cannot recall the specific villages or areas indicated, I do recall that these documents showed the presence of tanks where I knew there were no tanks or other military hardware present." Do you see that before you in your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. Not only that, I pointed that out to the senior UNMO when I showed him that plan, to Steinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Putting aside the fact that you can't identify the villages or areas, were you in those villages or areas on either the 4th or the 5th of August, 1995, during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if you weren't in those villages or those areas, you don't know whether or not -- well, you don't know whether or not a mobile vehicle, such as a tank, was in that village on the 4th or the 5th, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to tanks, there were other positions indicated on that map that did not exist in reality, at least not until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tchernetsky, the question was whether, not being present in those villages, whether you knew or did not know whether or not there was a mobile vehicle, such as a tank, in that village or those villages on the 4th or the 5th August. Do you know? Don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the presence or absence of mobile military hardware in those population centre, I certainly couldn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go back to these villages and areas after you got this report and do a shelling analysis; and if so, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not go back there with that specific objective. I did not receive such an assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in this respect. Did you return to those villages at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I mean to say those villages remained in your areas of responsibility mand we continued to control them after Operation Storm, to inspect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever find any mobile vehicle, such as a tank, which was apparently not able to function anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither before nor after the operation, there was no mobile military equipment in those population centres that were mentioned. We did not find any, and we didn't find any damaged equipment either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tchernetsky, the areas that you were talking about after Operation Storm came under the control of the Republic of Croatia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the documents that you allegedly found, you found at the end of September 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember dates. I've said so before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it was well after Operation Storm, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was well after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by point of clarification, Judge, that this was what he was talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What you're talking about in these alleged documents was targets that you supposedly saw on a piece of paper that were from prior to Operation Storm, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was called plan of artillery preparation for that area, so that document concerned the preparatory stage of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll move to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know I have a limited time and maybe I can handle this across the bar, because it was an issue that came up during the course of the testimony of the witness. A document was received in evidence which is - actually, it was received by the Defence, D65, and Mr. Russo touched upon it - which is a CIVPOL report of August 12, 1995, concerning the homicides of Mile Milivojevic and Ilija Milivojevic. We discussed that previously. I'm a little asking for Your Honours' guidance in this sense on these particular issues, given the fact that the autopsy reports from Ilija Milivojevic is D7, and that was entered into evidence with a cause of death being unascertained at autopsy. Mile Milivojevic, which is D8, his, likewise, has an uncertain death. The UN CIVPOL report notes, in D635, that it is impossible to see how the two men died. That is the centre of the item. Then in the clarification schedule, filed by the Office of the Prosecutor pursuant to Your Honour's instructions, the notation in the clarification schedule of the murders notes that the cause of death is uncertain. That is a document filed by the Office of the Prosecutor on 29 March 2007. I raise this issue in from the standpoint of the Defence being prepared to meet the evidence, yet it is unclear notwithstanding some questions in this regard exactly what we are meeting. The OTP is uncertain as to the cause of death, the autopsy report has no cause of death, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's created six years after the event, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it is. The autopsy report -- well, I submit to the Your Honour that a shot to the cranium would be evident until the cranium --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will leave traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is in conjunction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You ask our specific attention for the several sources of information we have on the potential causes of death or the causes of death unknown in relation to these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can be a bit more precise, to answer the first question, Judge, and it goes to the CIVPOL report received in evidence, D65, from the 12th of December, which notes that the police officers at the time were impossible to see how the two men died. It just makes it -- excuse me. I apologise, it is 12th of August, 2005. In an effort to meet the evidence presented by the Office of the Prosecutor, i.e., through the 65 ter statements of this witness or the exhibits, it renders it virtually impossible to answer, when there is no cause of death not only from the autopsy, but also from the particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is rather argumentative, what we could conclude from what pieces of evidence. Of course, we have heard only part of the case, but these appears to be important sources of information. Now, what would you ask the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly, with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not going to show all the reports. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour -- JUDGE ORIE -- exactly the type of exercise which I discourage you to make, to give the full information then ask the witness to draw inferences which finally the Chamber will have to draw on the basis of the complete evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking the question because I'm accepting your discouragement, and I simply raise this issue because at this particular juncture, on this particular scheduled killing, it is impossible to know what the Defence is called upon to meet because it is impossible to know what the Prosecution's position is when there is no cause of death and there is this type of convicting information. In the normal course of events, and certainly we wouldn't do that, we would go through the litany of questions. But I understand Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not what this witness could add to that. I see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask him whether he is certain about what he observed or not, and say that there were other reports which says that cause of death was unknown, and whether he sticks to what he knows about it. Then that's approximately where it ends, unless you have specific reasons to believe that there are certain aspects in the testimony of this witness which could be attacked thoroughly on the basis of these documents. For example, if the documents say he was shot to the left of the head, and if the witness would have said to the right, that could ask very specific points, but I leave it finally up to you. What I want to avoid is that if the witness is clear in what he says he has seen, that we put all the pieces of information and then say, You must be right, isn't it? That, of course, finally is not a way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I raise the issue, Judge, simply, I'm sure you appreciate the difficulties from the Defence side of answering a homicide when the cause of death is uncertain. That's the difficulty. To the extent that if we eliminate this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I correct you. It's difficult. Cause of death can be established by all means of evidence, and you have drawn your attention specifically now to the fact that experts in autopsies and other documents say that the authors of those documents could not establish a cause of death. That is not the same as no cause of death. That's for the Chamber finally to decide on what basis of what evidence we will or we will not accept that a person died due to a specific cause of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to this, this is my last question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the particular incident that took place on the 12th of August, where you supposedly saw these two bodies, you note in P204 on page 4, the first full paragraph, and you said that: "Because of the fact that our office was close to that house, I went to the site and was present when the bodies were removed." Now, in fact, sir, you were not present when those bodies were removed, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the bodies were being removed, I was at the office; and since the office is next to that house, I observed the whole thing, the whole process. I had just come back from a patrol. At the beginning at the request of our landlady, me and the Polish colleague entered the house. We saw the dead bodies. After that, we reported to the sector staff about it, the sector south told me to turn it over to the UN CIVPOL, and further investigation was conducted by UN CIVPOL. But the bodies were removed eventually by the Croatian police and by an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tchernetsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a question. Could, please, D152 be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we turn to the last five pages of this document. Mr. Tchernetsky, do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the list of the RSK soldiers that I found in Podinarje and subsequently turned over to Croatian authorities with participation of other international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you -- do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page, please. Could you tell us what it is, and whether this is also your signature?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This page was also signed by me. This is the list of civilians of persons that we found in Podinarje and recorded, registered. Subsequently, most of these people were sent to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we move to the next page. Could you confirm that this is -- could you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is one of the lists. I wouldn't be able to say exactly from which area; perhaps Podinarje again. This could be just another copy, just in handwriting -- handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a similar list? It is apparently not the same list, is it?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list from a different region, Your Honours. As I told you, we also looked for people in that area, registered them, and then provided humanitarian and medical assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then move to the last page of this document. The signature on this page, which is still in front of you, is yours as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My signature, again, and the date is 18th of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the last page. Your signature as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... similar list?

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I said to the last page, but I have forgotten one, I'm afraid. The previous one would be the same questions in relation to this list.

utterances.speaker: ALEXANDER TCHERNETSKY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My signature. This is a list that I provided to investigators as a sample of the kind of work that we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I asked the witness these questions because D152 was admitted into evidence; and to that statement, which is the same statement as P204, that statement, the T1 to T5 were attached where they are not attached to P204, which apart from these attachments is the same statement. In the statements, T1 to T5, where we find those markings on these documents, are mentioned. So, therefore, we have at this moment D152 that is the statement of Mr. Tchernetsky. Date of the interview is 18th of May 2002, with five pages attached to it, admitted into evidence. We, at that time, said that we would review whether admission was appropriate on the basis of the attestation of the witness if it would appear. The witness has not only attested to the statement itself, but also now to the five attached pages to it. Of course, we could now do a rather complex exercise to get rid of P204, but let's leave it for the time being as it is. D152 is the May 2002 statement of Mr. Tchernetsky with the attachments, and P204 is the same statement but now without the attachments. That was the purpose of this short exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the parties would agree that on the basis of the evidence just given by the witness, that there is no reason to review the decision to admit D152? Yes. I see all the parties agree with that. Mr. Tchernetsky, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I hope you have a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Tchernetsky out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the -- Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to inform the Court that -- you mentioned there is a formal procedure for revisiting the transcript, translation issues. I have been informed by one of the Russian colleagues on our team that the witness's references to the word "control" in indicating movements of the UNMOs, that he was actually saying "monitor." In any event, I would like the Court's guidance on exactly how to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. If you have any reason to believe that what we see on our English transcript is not reflecting accurately what the witness said, and if it is an issue which is of sufficient importance to be corrected, then please tell us exactly, page, line, et cetera, and then we could apply for a review of, first of all, what was said and then how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We'll do that in a written submission, Your Honour, if that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you make a brief written submission, then it can be passed on to CLSS, and if need be to the audio visual unit, and then you'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Russo, usually, it is better to do these kind of things when the witness is still there, because if the parties would agree on that there might be a flaw or a shortcoming - and I emphasise that I'm always surprised how little, how small the number of requests is and, therefore, how excellent the quality of work of our interpreters is - but if there is any reason to raise such an issue, preferably to be done when the witness is still there, or seek clarification in re-examination, asking, When you use that word, what do you mean by it exactly, et cetera. Then that saves us the risk of having to recall the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be reviewing that to, first of all, determine whether or not it is a matter of sufficient weight, and I will certainly address the Defence on that before approaching the Court with a written submission, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Now, before we start with the next witness, I was informed that there was a procedural issue to be raised before the witness enters the courtroom. I must admit that I haven't brought yet my material for the next witness, so it could well be that I'm unable to fully understand what the issue is. But let's hear from you, Mr. Kehoe. Can we deal with the matter in -- the next witness will give his testimony in open session without protective measures from what I understand. It will be Witness 110. Mr. Kehoe, what is the issue you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The issue is concerning the series of UN CIVPOL reports that are -- that the Office of the Prosecutor is attempting to tender. I took the -- well, laboured through the actual reports in congestion with Mr. Elleby's 92 ter statements. Any number of these documents, and there are approximately over 60, as I go through them, there are numerous documents that Mr. Elleby says, "I don't know anything about them because I wasn't even there." He left on October 1st of 1995. He says, "It looks whatever it is, but I wasn't there." That encompasses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's quite a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Quite a number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... there has been communication bout two series of documents, the ones when he wasn't there and the other ones which he did not personally observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or that he doesn't anything about, better still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It would be different if, in fact, they got back and they sat around and there was some consultation about a particular item, but his 92 ter statement says that he doesn't know anything about them. Obviously, on those particular exhibits, those particular CIVPOL reports, we are objecting to their admission through this witness for those reasons. There are documents that -- I mean, then there are a series of documents that they intend to propose that are frankly in line with what one of the other protected witnesses that testified here then backed off of during or prior to the testimony when the Office of the Prosecutor came in and said when this witness said he saw all these bodies, he really didn't. Those are some of the documents that the Prosecution attempts to bring into evidence. Suffice it to say, Judge, I mean, with regard to cross-examination, it is difficult, of course, to cross-examine a witness where on these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... quite easy, isn't it? He can't tell us anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I guess the difficulty then comes in, and I guess what happened last week is a good example of that, is when we deal with an individual scheduled killing like we have, where this person gives this story about having seen all these bodies, and then when you talk to the person or the Office of the Prosecutor talks to them on the eve of coming in here, and they said: Well, I didn't see those bodies at all"; when, in fact, they used it as count in indictment, as well as part of the clarification schedule. It just makes it very difficult and virtually impossible to cross on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, if the witness doesn't know anything about it, it is rather easy; although, the Chamber has a difficulty then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully agree with you that if it would admitted into evidence, that what wight to be given to that material is not an easy matter. I think that is it even more difficult than the difficulties you face during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I didn't mean to be selfish and just discuss my position. I understand the position of the Trial Chamber. But from the standpoint of the Defence, I just wanted the Court to appreciate my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be honest, of course, we'll consider the matter over the break, and I couldn't say that we were not aware of this type of objection to be expected. But we'll use the break now to see whether your objection should result in non-admission of these documents. We have a list of which specific documents you oppose against and the two categories, the one is he wasn't there anymore and the other one was he didn't observe personally on what was reported. Could I ask: From the submissions made by the parties, I have no information yet that the other Defence teams would join in this objections. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. We have no particular interest in information within those documents, so it wasn't a matter which concerned us, but the submission by Mr. Kehoe we would support entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have one other aspect. It's not that particular problem, but just an agreement with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But, first, to conclude this aspect. Do you think you've made your position sufficiently clear. That's just for us because we'll consider the matter and we'll decide the matter. So, therefore, I just want to be sure that where you took only a couple of minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Judge, I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting to you keep talking, but I want to make sure. I mean, this is an important issue. You are seeking to the non-admission of quite a number of documents; and, therefore, I want to verify whether you think that you have explained your position sufficiently and whether you got the impression that the Chamber understood your submissions sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the -- Your Honour, has the crux -- the Bench has the crux of our position on those documents. I don't want to belabour that point. I mean, these documents are documents that could come in through other witnesses, where we would be able to talk about some of the other matters contained therein, as opposed to somebody that doesn't know anything about them. But Your Honours that the kernel of the argument presented by the Defence. I do have one other item --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- with regard to the summary of the dossier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the summaries on the on the Excel sheet, were the summaries are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like one of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What is the purpose of tendering that into evidence where there is a dispute whether the summary is right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had not intended to send that in as an item of substantive evidence. I was simply responding to the Court's concern expressed earlier about voluminous documentation, and pointed to the Court the portions of the documents that we thought were at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there agreement between the parties that your summary is not what we should look at, but, if we admit into evidence these documents, that we should look at the documents and that a summary is the just an effort to assist with us a risk to confuse us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge. I talked to Mr. Tieger about this last night, and we agree at this time that the summary aspect of this document would be removed and that we would work with the Prosecutor to come up with a summary that's in there. We have done that with regard to the other documents, and we are just going to duplicate that. So, in the not too distant future, we will have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noted now what Excell can do for you, that is, sorting, taking out portions, adding portions, is now fully explored. We'll consider the objections. We will wait until we see the new Excel sheet with other information as agreed between the parties. Any other matter before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, would it proper if I just now respond briefly to the Defence objections, or would it be better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may do that, and I apologise for not having invited you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon, Your Honours. I think the position of the Prosecution, with respect to the admission of several documents and with respect to similar documents in the past, has been clear. We are not seeking to admit these documents based on the witness's knowledge about the incidents or any presence that he may have been in Knin or not at the time, but based on his position as a Sector South chief of CIVPOL and his position to authenticate these documents by the way they were formatted, they were reported, they were formulated, et cetera. So there are other factors that go to admissibility of these documents. We never purported to say that the witness knew actually anything about these documents which would, indeed, go to the weight of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, more or less, say it is more than tendering them from the bar table, although the witness may not have detailed knowledge about the documents but he may have been informed about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Documents, on their face, are sufficient, I believe, to be admitted on their face across the bar table. But in addition, the witness authenticates them and explains the reporting procedure, which adds somewhat to their admissibility, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kehoe, just for our information, is there any specific reason to be very cautious about the authenticity of the documents as such, or is there any reason to believe that there's any forgery involved? I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Judge, none whatsoever. I did not -- and if I made that kind of inference, I didn't mean that in any fashion. I'm just talking about simply, as an advocate, representing our client just being able to meet this evidence. You know, that is the crux of the argument, as I said, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. We will have a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00 and then we have one hour with the witness. Will it be you, Ms. Frolich, who examines this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered how to proceed with the objections you raised and that were joined by the other Defence counsel. We'll proceed in the following way -- Ms. Frolich has disappeared behind the lectern, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I was not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now ... Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The drilling has not stopped yet. Security is trying to find the culprit. Ms. Frolich, The next witness to appear, which is Witness known until now as Witness 110, Mr. Elleby, I take it that in the beginning of his testimony, you will seek the attestation in order to have his statement admitted under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are invited to put in this context a few questions to the witness in relation to what you seek him to establish, in relation to the documents, the attached documents. I do understand that you say that he may recognise the format, or he may have reviewed them and not seen any persons which he is not aware of, or whatever. But what you explained to us earlier, what your purpose was to establish through this witness, not, as far as I understand, the truth of the content, at least not in relation it those documents Mr. Kehoe is objecting to, that is, the documents that were created when the witness wasn't there anymore, or the documents where the witness has no personal knowledge of the events described in the documents. Now, you are invited to do that in relation to a selection you can make yourself: One example out of the first series, that is, where the witness wasn't there anymore. Another example out of the second series Mr. Kehoe objected to. That is not to take hours, but just try it find, I take it, that you want him to confirm that this is the format used, and that, well, whatever you consider relevant in this respect. The Chamber would not expect this to take anything more than perhaps two or three minutes. The Defence, before we finally decide on admission, will have an opportunity to put similar questions but also limited to that aspect, not other aspects, and then the Chamber will decide on admission of the statement and the annexes. This is the procedural solution the Chamber has established now, and then we'll give a decision. It might well be that if we would decide whether it will be admission or non-admission of these two series, that we would write down the reasons later, so reasons to follow. The Chamber reserves its position in that respect, whether we would immediately give the full reasons for such a decision. Is it clear to you? Clear to you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge. I don't want to belabour the point. I mean, obviously, I don't want it ask unnecessary questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're always invited not to ask unnecessary questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My questions candidly, Judge, would be limited to what I laid out in our motion, which is: Mr. Elleby, you weren't here at the time, or you don't know anything about this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two shorts questions, perhaps two short answers. You even could agree on this with Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I got my information from the supplemental 92 ter statement -- not the supplemental, the second 92 ter statement where I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is that, of course, I fully understand your tradition, that you put the question: Isn't it true that you left that day and isn't it true that this document comes from a later day and isn't it true that this day is after the first day? But you also could say, I've got no further questions, where it is apparent that the witness had left already on the basis of his 92 ter statement. Let's try to deal with it as efficiently as possible, but we want to give a fair opportunity to understand exactly how Ms. Frolich wants to introduce these documents, and to give a fair opportunity to Defence. For example, if she chooses an example which gives a totally different format what we usually see, then, of course, you could challenge that issue as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in review of these documents, I don't think the format is too different. I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not start guessing about it. It might that be Ms. Frolich has a perfect format or a non-perfect format. We'll see. Ms. Frolich, are you ready to call the next witness, which the Chamber understands will be Jan Elleby?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Elleby, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, first of all, can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you, and I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Elleby.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: First of all, with the assistance of the usher, of hard copies of the witness statements could be provided to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: My full name is Jan Elleby.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you give four statements to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on 17th September, 1995, and that is 65 ter 4867; 14 September 1997, and that is 65 ter 4868; 10th October 2005, 65 ter 4869; and 19th and 20th February, 2008, which is supplemental witness statement, 65 ter number 4870.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you have these four statements in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: After your statements were recorded, did you have a chance to read them in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you sign the English copies of these statements?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review these statements, in the language that you understand, the day before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to make corrections to a couple of these statements?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I have permission to lead the witness through these corrections that he has made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is no objection from the defence, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, in your 1997 statement, on page 2 - that's also page 2 in B/C/S, 65 ter 4868 - you mentioned you had meetings with Mr. Romanic two to three times a week. Did you, in fact, have only two to three meetings in total with him?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In the same statement, on page 3 - that's page 2 in B/C/S - you mentioned receiving 15 to 20 reports of burnt houses everyday from 5th August to the 1st of October. Can you, from this distance in time, confirm that number?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: No. I cannot confirm the number of written reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. In your 2008 supplemental statement, in paragraph 6 - that is 65 ter 4870 - you mentioned there were 30 to 50 CIVPOL monitors in Sector South after Operation Storm. Did you, in fact, mean to say that there were 25 to 30 monitors?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And when you authenticated -- in the same supplemental statement, when you authenticated the document under 65 ter number 662, which is the 18th of August, 1995 damage assessment document, you said you could observe more damage in Knin than noted in that report. Is that, in fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What would be your observation based -- what would be your -- what you say about the amount much damage that you could observe in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: The amount of damage mentioned in the text in the document is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just remind that you since you and I are both speaking the same language here, if you make a short break between each question and answer, so that the court reporters can keep up with us.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, taking into account these corrections, do these statements taken together accurately and truthfully, to the best of your knowledge, reflect what you said at the time that the statements were being taken?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Would you give the same answers today if you were examined on the same matters?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I would ask that these four statements be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Ms. Frolich, of course, we have not seen them. The witness has apparently statements in front of him. Could we just have them on the screen, if only the first pages, so that we can identify those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I wanted to save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But this should be kind of a practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, do you see on the screen in front of you -- what do you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is no problem leading the witness there, but just to have them on the screen. Also, Mr. Registrar, that we're not talking -- that we're talking about same statements and about nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Elleby, is this your 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And I believe that is 65 ter number 4867. And if we could go to -- Mr. President, should I show the page where witness signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you show him at one spot or perhaps at the end his signature, that would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, is this -- is this the statement -- is this the last page of your statement, and do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: It's not my signature, but it is the last page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we move on to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any place where he has put a signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No. I believe, on this statement, that there is no signature of Mr. Elleby, but he has confirmed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this is the statement that you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If we could move on to 65 ter 4868.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, is this your 14 September 1997 statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And is this your signature at the bottom of the page, in English version?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, you earlier referred to the September 1995 statement, where, I take it, you wanted to refer to the 17th of September, 1995 statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and where this is the statement given the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Jan Elleby was an UNCIVPOL, or United Nations Civilian Police, monitor in Sector South in Knin, from mid-May to the end of September 1995. In his capacity as the deputy chief and later chief of CIVPOL in Sector South, he was familiar with the reporting system within UNCIVPOL, its structure, mandate, and monitoring system. The mandate of CIVPOL was to monitor the work of the Croatian civilian police and report human rights abuses. Mr. Elleby received incident reports from CIVPOL monitors in the sector and forwarded them to CIVPOL headquarters in Zagreb. His main task was to inform the Croatian civilian police of the incidents reported by his monitors and supervise his staff who also reported incidents themselves to the police, attend meetings with the chiefs of police administration for Knin and Zadar, and monitor their responses. He authenticates a number of CIVPOL incident reports and other CIVPOL-related documents. Mr. Elleby was in Knin during and after the shelling attack on 4th and 5th August 1995. He provides evidence about the pattern of shelling and its effect on the civilian population. He provides evidence about HV soldiers and civilian police looting and burning in Knin in the aftermath of the shelling, the restrictions of movement placed on the UN personnel, and the reasons given by Croatian authorities for the restrictions. The witness observed graves in the Knin cemetery. He also observed burning and destruction outside of Knin in the town of Kistanje and on the road from Knin to Drnis. Mr. Elleby provides evidence that neither the military nor the civilian police did anything to stop the looting and destruction, that the Croatian civilian police did very little or nothing in response to notice of the crimes committed that was provided by CIVPOL, and that they largely ignored the reports or denied Croat responsibility. The Croatian military authorities had full control of the area in Knin and its surrounds during the first few days of Operation Storm, and no one else but the military authorities had access to it. Mr. Elleby also observed members of the Croatian special police in Knin and heard about the special police closing off areas during clean-up operations. That concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: CIVPOL was structured with a headquarter in Zagreb, and there was a commissioner to whom I was subordinated as a sector chief. When I was a deputy sector chief, I was subordinated to the sector chief in Sector South which was Mr. Norman Boucher from Canada. We did restructure in Sector South after Operation Storm; and in the headquarter, there were some coordinators subordinated to me, and we had under the headquarter some CIVPOL stations where it was a station commander and some monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And could you tell us what relationship of CIVPOL to other UN agencies was?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: Yes. CIVPOL was just one of more branches in the headquarter in Knin. There was a military, of course, and the head of headquarter was a general. Then there was CIVPOL, we had UNHCR, Red Cross administrations. I don't remember if there were anymore. Anyway, there was morning meetings everyday where the general sat at the end of the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could you explain the relationship of subordination that is shown in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: In the sector, after I became a sector chief, there was a deputy who was assisting me, and the coordinators were responsible for one area each. No matter what the incident was, there was investigation, operations, or human rights, and they were reporting to me what was going on in the -- in their area of responsibility. They got the knowledge from station commanders which, again, got their knowledge from -- from the monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who reported incidents to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY
utterances.text: There were more levels of information, and the station -- the UNCIVPOL station commanders had contact with the Croatian police. The coordinators had contact with the Croatian police. And I had some meetings with the head of police in Knin and -- and the officer he was subordinated to in Zadar, and I also had meetings with a high level officer in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, I'm looking at the clock, and I'd like to adjourn for the day. Before I do so, Mr. Gotovina, Mr. Cermak, and Mr. Markac, there might be some delays in your transportation to the detention unit for very practical and good reasons. So if you have to wait a bit longer than usual, just be informed that there are practical reasons which do not allow to do it any quicker. Then we will adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow, 22nd of May, in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of May, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
